params.question: Which inflammatory cell is the primary driver of the late-phase response and airway remodelling in bronchial asthma?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutrophils are the predominant inflammatory cells in COPD, not asthma. In COPD, cigarette smoke activates neutrophils and macrophages, leading to a protease–antiprotease imbalance that destroys alveolar walls.

Mast cells initiate the early-phase response through IgE-mediated degranulation, releasing histamine and leukotrienes. However, the late-phase response 6–12 hours later and subsequent remodelling are driven by eosinophils.

Correct. Eosinophils dominate the late-phase response in asthma, arriving 6–12 hours after allergen exposure. IL-5 drives their production and survival, and repeated eosinophilic inflammation causes the airway remodelling that leads to fixed obstruction.
Macrophages play a key role in COPD pathophysiology alongside neutrophils. In asthma, the dominant late-phase cell is the eosinophil — this distinction is central to choosing the right drug class.

overallFeedback.feedback: The late-phase response in asthma is driven by eosinophils, not neutrophils or mast cells. Remember: asthma = eosinophils, COPD = neutrophils — this distinction directly guides drug selection.
Correct! Eosinophils are the hallmark inflammatory cell of asthma, distinguishing it from the neutrophil-driven inflammation of COPD.

params.question: Long-acting beta-2 agonists such as salmeterol can be safely used as the sole maintenance bronchodilator in both asthma and COPD.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. LABA monotherapy is safe in COPD but contraindicated in asthma. LABAs used without an inhaled corticosteroid have been linked to increased asthma-related mortality — always combine LABA with ICS in asthma.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. While LABA monotherapy is acceptable in COPD, it is dangerous in asthma. Studies showed increased asthma-related deaths when LABAs were used without an inhaled corticosteroid. In asthma, LABAs must always be combined with ICS.

interactions.label: A medical student with allergic rhinitis reports that cetirizine has controlled

params.question: A medical student with allergic rhinitis reports that cetirizine has controlled her sneezing and itching, but her nasal congestion remains troublesome. What is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching to a first-generation antihistamine would add sedation without improving congestion. Both first- and second-generation antihistamines act on histamine H1 receptors, and nasal congestion is driven primarily by alpha-adrenergic pathways, not histamine.

Correct. Intranasal corticosteroids address all four symptom domains of allergic rhinitis — sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea, and congestion — because they suppress the broad inflammatory process rather than just the histamine pathway.

answers.text: Prescribe oral pseudoephedrine for long-term daily use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While decongestants relieve congestion by constricting alpha-receptor-controlled nasal vessels, they are unsuitable for long-term use. Topical decongestants beyond five days cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa), and oral agents carry cardiovascular risks.

Leukotriene receptor antagonists have a modest role in allergic rhinitis but are less effective than intranasal corticosteroids for congestion. They are generally reserved as add-on therapy, not first-line for persistent nasal blockage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Nasal congestion is driven by alpha-adrenergic pathways, not histamine H1 receptors, which is why antihistamines alone leave it untreated. Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective addition because they suppress the broad inflammatory process.
Correct! Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single drug class for allergic rhinitis because they suppress inflammation across all four symptom domains.

interactions.label: A patient with pneumonia is producing thick, purulent sputum. He requests a code

params.question: A patient with pneumonia is producing thick, purulent sputum. He requests a codeine-based cough suppressant to help him sleep. Why should this request be declined?

answers.text: Codeine is absolutely contraindicated in all patients with pneumonia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Codeine is not absolutely contraindicated in pneumonia per se. The concern here relates to the nature of the cough itself — it is productive and performing a protective function that should not be suppressed.

answers.text: Suppressing a productive cough impairs mucociliary clearance of infected secretions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When a cough is productive, the reflex is performing useful work clearing secretions from the airways. Suppressing it with an antitussive can lead to sputum retention and worsening infection. The appropriate approach is to facilitate clearance with expectorants, mucolytics, and hydration.

answers.text: Codeine interacts with standard antibiotic regimens for pneumonia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Codeine does not have clinically significant interactions with most antibiotics used for pneumonia. The reason to avoid it here relates to the productive nature of the cough, not a drug interaction.

answers.text: Antitussives can only act on dry cough receptors and would be pharmacologically ineffective

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antitussives can suppress both dry and productive cough at the receptor level — they raise the cough reflex threshold regardless of cause. The issue is not efficacy but safety: suppressing a productive cough impairs the clearance mechanism the body needs.

overallFeedback.feedback: In productive cough, the cough reflex is doing useful protective work clearing secretions. Suppressing it with an antitussive like codeine can trap infected material in the airways and worsen the underlying condition.
Correct! Productive cough is protective. The goal is to facilitate clearance — not suppress the reflex.

interactions.label: A 52-year-old non-smoking woman on enalapril for hypertension presents with a pe

params.question: A 52-year-old non-smoking woman on enalapril for hypertension presents with a persistent dry cough for ten weeks. Her chest X-ray is normal. Applying the structured approach to cough management, what is the most appropriate first step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting symptomatic therapy without identifying the underlying cause is the most common prescribing error in chronic cough management. The structured approach requires treating the cause first; symptomatic therapy is added only if still needed afterward.

answers.text: Investigate for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with a pH study

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GERD is one of the three common causes of chronic cough in non-smokers with a normal chest X-ray, but the structured approach requires addressing the most obvious remediable cause first. This patient is taking an ACE inhibitor — a well-recognised cause of chronic dry cough.

answers.text: Discontinue enalapril and reassess after four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ACE inhibitor-induced cough affects up to 15% of patients and typically resolves within one to four weeks of stopping the drug. The structured approach mandates identifying and treating the underlying cause before adding symptomatic therapy. Switching to an ARB is the standard substitution.

answers.text: Start empirical inhaled corticosteroids for possible cough-variant asthma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cough-variant asthma is in the differential for chronic cough, but starting empirical ICS before addressing the ACE inhibitor would bypass the most straightforward and reversible intervention. Discontinue enalapril first, then reassess.

overallFeedback.feedback: The structured approach to chronic cough requires identifying the underlying cause before adding symptomatic therapy. In a patient on an ACE inhibitor with an unexplained dry cough and normal chest X-ray, discontinuing the drug and reassessing is the logical first step.
Correct! The structured approach identifies and treats the cause first. ACE inhibitor cough is the most readily reversible cause in this patient.
